title: How to integrate Google login feature in ASP.NET Core Identity
description: Add Google OAuth as an external login provider for ASP.NET Core Identity.

data.text: External login providers like Google, Facebook, and Microsoft let users sign in with existing accounts — no new password required. ASP.NET Core Identity has built-in OAuth middleware that handles the redirect, callback, and user creation flow.

terms.definition: An authorization framework that lets a user grant a third-party app access without sharing credentials. Google login uses OAuth 2.0.
Credentials issued by Google Cloud Console that identify your app in the OAuth flow.
A class that carries the claims and provider key returned by Google after the user authenticates.
The authentication scheme used for external login cookies during the OAuth handshake.

data.text: Step 1 — Set Up Google Cloud Console
Go to https://console.cloud.google.com and create a new project. Then navigate to APIs & Services > Credentials and create an OAuth 2.0 Client ID. Choose Web application and add your redirect URIs:

data.title: Port numbers must match
data.text: The redirect URIs in Google Cloud Console must exactly match the port your local dev server runs on. If the port changes, update both the Google Console and your code.
Save the generated Client ID and Client Secret — you will paste them into Program.cs.
Step 2 — Install the Google Auth Package

data.title: Install via NuGet Package Manager or dotnet CLI

data.text: Chain .AddGoogle() after .AddIdentity() in Program.cs. The SignInScheme must be IdentityConstants.ExternalScheme so Identity can handle the external login handshake.

data.title: Program.cs — register Google auth

data.text: Step 4 — Add GoogleLogin and GoogleResponse Actions

The GoogleLogin action initiates the OAuth handshake by returning a ChallengeResult. After Google authenticates the user, it redirects to GoogleResponse, where we check whether the user already exists or needs to be created.

data.title: AccountController — Google login actions

data.text: Add a 'Log in with Google' button to the standard login form. The button targets the GoogleLogin action.

data.caption: Google OAuth sign-in flow with ASP.NET Core Identity
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as ASP.NET Core App
    participant G as Google OAuth
    U->>A: Clicks 'Log in with Google'
    A->>G: Redirect to Google authorization endpoint
    G->>U: Shows Google sign-in page
    U->>G: Enters Google credentials
    G->>A: Redirect to /Account/GoogleResponse with code
    A->>G: Exchange code for token
    G->>A: Returns user claims (name, email)
    A->>A: ExternalLoginSignInAsync checks AspNetUsers
    alt User exists
        A->>U: Sign in — issue Identity cookie
    else User does not exist
        A->>A: CreateAsync + AddLoginAsync
        A->>U: Sign in — issue Identity cookie
    end

data.description: Wire up Google as an external login provider for an existing Identity project.
steps: Create a project in Google Cloud Console and get Client ID + Secret.
Call AddGoogle() in Program.cs with your credentials.
Add GoogleLogin and GoogleResponse actions to AccountController.
Add a 'Log in with Google' button to Login.cshtml.
Test the full flow: click Google button, sign in, get redirected back.
data.expectedOutcome: Users can sign in with their Google account. On first login a new Identity user is created; on subsequent logins the existing account is found and signed in.

items.text: OAuth 2.0 Client ID created in Google Cloud Console

items.hint: Both must use the exact localhost port.

items.text: GoogleResponse handles new and existing users
items.hint: ExternalLoginSignInAsync checks; CreateAsync + AddLoginAsync for new users.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: AddGoogle() registers Google as an OAuth 2.0 external provider.
GoogleLogin returns a ChallengeResult to start the handshake.
GoogleResponse handles both new user creation and returning user sign-in.
ExternalLoginSignInAsync checks AspNetUserLogins for an existing association.
data.takeaway: Your users can now sign in with Google. Next, learn to work with claims for fine-grained authorization.
